# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting protects the stability and reliability of your APIs. This page covers how the Gateway handles it.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and includes a `Retry-After` header indicating how many seconds to wait, which tells the client to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

These settings let you balance protecting your services against keeping the experience smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones can seem like magic, but they rely on destructive interference. They don't only block sound. They fight sound with sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the ambient noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that is the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, reducing what reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

Noise cancellation comes down to physics and engineering working together. If you fly often, work remotely, or just like quiet, knowing how it works can help you choose a pair.

final: The relationship between remote work and employee productivity remains a hotly debated topic in organizational research. Okafor et al. (2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). These benefits, though, appear to depend heavily on task type: as Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution, "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). These findings point to a need for researchers to examine the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

As the sun broke through the fog outside, Nora realized that her father had never really been gone. He lived on in every gear and spring, in the patience he had taught her, in the steady rhythm of time itself. Grief, she understood now, was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

# Rate Limiting

The Gateway rate limits requests to keep your APIs stable and reliable. This page explains how it works and how to configure it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header that says how many seconds to wait. Clients should treat it as a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

Note that `burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but they run on a pretty neat idea: destructive interference. They don't just block sound. They fight it with more sound.

Here's what's going on. Small microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly pick up the noise around you. A chip then produces a sound wave that's a mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

It works best on steady, low-pitched sounds, like an airplane engine's hum or an air conditioner's drone, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, like a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also count on the ear cushions sealing out sound passively.

So noise cancellation really comes down to physics and engineering working together. If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like peace and quiet, knowing how it works can help you choose better.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog was sitting on Delancey Street and the air smelled like rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. Her chest went tight.

Nothing was different. Dozens of clocks covered the walls, all their pendulums swinging together, unhurried. On the workbench was the pocket watch he'd been fixing when the stroke got him. The back was still open, and one tiny screw sat next to it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door showed up in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said quietly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

When he'd gone, Nora sat down at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands were shaking. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers remembered anyway. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch started to tick.

Outside, the sun broke through the fog, and it hit her that her father wasn't really gone. He was there in every gear and spring, in the patience he'd taught her, in the steady rhythm of time itself. Grief, she understood now, was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, his name was still above the shop door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you spend much time working on computers, sooner or later you'll run into a task you wish you could automate. Maybe you need to search and replace across a huge pile of text files, or rename and shuffle around a bunch of photos in some complicated way. Maybe you want to write a small custom database, a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

And if you're a professional software developer, you might be juggling several C/C++/Java libraries and finding that the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is just too slow. Maybe you're writing a test suite for one of those libraries and the testing code is tedious to write. Or maybe you've built a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement an entire new language for it.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or some Windows batch files for a few of these jobs, but shell scripts are best at moving files around and changing text data. They're not well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program instead, but even a first draft can take a lot of development time. Python is simpler to use, runs on Windows, macOS, and Unix, and will help you get the job done faster.

Python lets you split your program into modules that you can reuse in other Python programs. It also comes with a large collection of standard modules you can build your programs on, or use as examples when you're learning to program in Python. Some of them handle things like file I/O, system calls, and sockets, and there are even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

Say a picture had come back from the frame-maker's and was leaning in the dining-room, waiting to be hung. Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, leave that to *me*. None of you needs to worry about it. *I'll* take care of all that."

Then he'd take off his coat and get started. He'd send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, then send one of the boys after her to tell her what size to buy. From there he'd work his way down, bit by bit, until the whole house was stirred up.

"Now, Will, go and get me my hammer," he'd shout. "Tom, you bring me the rule. I'll want the step-ladder, and I'd better have a kitchen chair too. And Jim! Run round to Mr. Goggles and tell him, 'Pa sends his kind regards, hopes your leg is better, and could he borrow your spirit-level?' Don't you go, Maria, because I'll need somebody to hold the light. And when the girl gets back, she'll have to go out again for a bit of picture-cord. And Tom! Where's Tom? Tom, come here. I'll want you to hand me up the picture."

Then he'd pick up the picture and drop it, and it would fall out of the frame. He'd try to save the glass and cut himself, and then he'd leap around the room hunting for his handkerchief. He couldn't find it, because it was in the pocket of the coat he'd taken off, and he had no idea where he'd put the coat. So everyone in the house had to stop looking for his tools and start looking for his coat, while he danced around them, getting in the way.
<<<END>>>

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting protects your APIs from being overwhelmed by any single client. This page explains how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait before retrying.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones work through destructive interference: they fight sound with sound rather than simply blocking it.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, dramatically reducing what reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly often, work remotely, or just value peace and quiet, knowing this can help you choose a pair more wisely.

(2018) conducted a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner," Nora said.

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. He wasn't gone, not really. He was in every gear and spring, in the patience he had taught her, in the steady tick of the shop. Grief was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. "Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

title: Rate limiting
sidebar_position: 4
---

The Gateway rate limits requests per client to keep your APIs stable and reliable.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header that says how many seconds to wait before retrying.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones work by destructive interference. Instead of only blocking sound, they cancel it with more sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the ambient noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that is the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, which greatly reduces what reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

Knowing this can help you choose a pair, whether you fly often or work from home.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Dozens of clocks still lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner," Nora said.

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, and her hands shook, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. She thought her father was still there, in the gears and springs and in the patience he had taught her. Grief, she thought, was love with nowhere to go. For now, it had somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there's some task you'd like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you'd like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you're a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you're writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you've written a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and are not well suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting protects your APIs from clients that send too many requests. This page explains how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and includes a `Retry-After` header with the number of seconds to wait. Clients should treat it as a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Use these settings to balance protecting your services against keeping things smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but they run on destructive interference. They fight sound with sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup keep sampling the noise around you. A dedicated chip builds a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less reaches your ears.

It works best on low, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises are much harder to cancel. A baby crying, a door slamming. That's why most headphones also lean on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

So the engine drone fades, but the slammed door still gets through.

final: Researchers still argue about whether remote work makes people more productive. Okafor et al. (2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees, and those assigned to work from home performed 13% better. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). Task type seems to matter a lot. So the open question is where the boundary conditions lie, and that's what researchers should dig into next.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. Her chest went tight.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks covered the walls, pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he'd been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora couldn't get a word out at first. Then: "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. She sat there listening. Her father wasn't really gone, she thought. He was in the gears and springs, and in the patience he'd taught her. Grief was love with nowhere to go. Now it had somewhere.

Years later the shop still had his name above the door. Nora wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

If you do much work on computers, sooner or later you'll find a task you'd like to automate. You might want to search and replace across a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a pile of photos in some complicated way. Or you'd like to write a small custom database, a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you're a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries and find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle too slow. Maybe you're writing a test suite for one of those libraries and the testing code is tedious. Or you've written a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a whole new language for it.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving files around and changing text data. They're not well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but even a first draft can take a lot of development time. Python is simpler to use, it's available on Windows, macOS, and Unix, and it will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python lets you split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples when you start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting keeps your APIs stable and reliable. This page explains how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and includes a `Retry-After` header telling the client how many seconds to wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

Note that `burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Tune these settings to balance protecting your services against giving your users a smooth experience.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but the idea behind them is simple: destructive interference. They don't just block sound. They fight it with more sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly pick up the noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

It works best on steady, low-frequency sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also depend on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like peace and quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a pair more wisely.

final: Whether remote work helps or hurts employee productivity is still a hotly debated question in organizational research. Okafor et al. (2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). But these benefits seem to depend heavily on the type of task: as Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution, "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). Researchers need to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door chimed the way it always had, and her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat closed up. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She hadn't touched a pair of tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

Outside, the sun broke through the fog. He wasn't really gone, Nora thought. He was in every gear and spring, in the patience he had taught her, in the steady rhythm of the room. Grief, she understood now, was just love with nowhere to go — until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you do much work on computers, sooner or later you'll run into a task you'd like to automate. Maybe you want to search and replace across a big pile of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photos in some complicated way. Maybe you'd like to write a small custom database, a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you're a professional software developer, you might be working with several C/C++/Java libraries and finding that the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Maybe you're writing a test suite for one of those libraries and the testing code is tedious to write. Or maybe you've got a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a whole new one just for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving files around and changing text data. They're not well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but even a first draft can take a lot of development time. Python is simpler to use, runs on Windows, macOS, and Unix, and will help you get the job done faster.

Python lets you split your program into modules that you can reuse in other Python programs. It also comes with a large collection of standard modules you can build your programs on, or use as examples when you're starting to learn Python. Some of these modules cover things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting keeps your APIs stable and reliable by capping how many requests each client can send. This page covers how the Gateway does it and how to configure it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and includes a `Retry-After` header indicating how many seconds the client should wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

Because `burst` defaults to 0, bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Adjust these settings to balance protecting your services against keeping things responsive for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but the idea behind them is fairly simple: destructive interference. Instead of just blocking sound, they fight it with more sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip then produces a sound wave that's the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and much less of the noise reaches your ears.

The technology works best on steady, low-frequency sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz: the hum of an airplane engine, say, or the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, like a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also depend on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

So it's physics, plus some clever engineering. If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like quiet, knowing how it works can help you pick the right pair.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora came back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door gave the same chime it always had, and something in her chest pulled tight.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks covered the walls, their pendulums swinging as patiently as ever. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he'd been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw sitting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said quietly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora had to swallow before she could answer. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

When he'd gone, Nora sat down at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands were shaking. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown, and the watch started to tick.

Outside, the sun was breaking through the fog. He hadn't really left, she thought. He was in every gear and spring, in the patience he'd taught her, in the steady beat of time itself. Maybe that was all grief was: love with nowhere to go. Now she had somewhere to put it.

Years later his name was still above the door, and every morning Nora still wound each clock, the way he always had.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate limiting

Rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable. This is how the Gateway handles it.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones can seem like magic, but the principle is simple: destructive interference. They fight sound with sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like quiet, knowing what the technology can and can't cancel makes it easier to choose a pair.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). The benefits appear to depend heavily on task type, though. Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution that "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). Researchers need to look harder at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain. The bell above the door chimed the way it always had.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in step. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he'd been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door came to the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "Every day. He was proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner." It came out smaller than she meant it to.

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

When he'd gone, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years, and her hands shook at first, but her fingers knew what to do. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun was coming through the fog outside. She didn't look up. She sat and listened to it run, one more small sound under all the others.

Years later, the shop still had his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and they’re not well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

The Gateway limits how many requests each client can make, which protects your APIs from being overloaded.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones work by destructive interference: they fight sound with sound.

Small microphones on the outside of each ear cup keep sampling the noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

The effect is strongest on steady, low-frequency sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also depend on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work remotely, or just like quiet, knowing this will help you choose a pair.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. Researchers need to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and everything smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. She had to stop a moment before she could go in.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door came to the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner." She couldn't look at him when she said it.

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years, and her hands were unsteady, but they knew what to do. Her father had taught her to go slowly, and she went slowly. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

It was a small sound among all the others. She was glad of it, and sorry, both at once. She stayed there until the sun broke through the fog.

Years later, the shop still had his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

- I kept the "Years later" coda as a short plain statement, without the tidy echo.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python lets you split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. "Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

# Rate limiting

The Gateway rate-limits requests per client to keep your APIs stable under load.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client goes over its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds the client should wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Tune these values to balance protecting your services against keeping requests flowing smoothly for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but the trick behind them is simple: they fight sound with more sound. The principle is called destructive interference.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup keep sampling the noise around you. A dedicated chip then produces a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase, so each peak of the new wave meets a trough of the noise. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less of the noise reaches your ears.

This works best on steady, low-frequency sound, generally below about 1,000 Hz: the hum of an airplane engine, the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden, high-pitched noises, like a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

Knowing this helps when you're choosing a pair. If what you want gone is a steady drone, the electronics will handle most of it. If it's sudden and sharp, you're depending largely on the cushions, so how well they seal matters as much as the chip.

final: Whether remote work makes employees more productive is still much debated in organizational research. In a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees, Okafor et al. (2018) found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A subsequent meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). These benefits appear to depend heavily on task type, however: as Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution, "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). Future research needs to pin down the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora came back to her father's shop, a thin fog was sitting on Delancey Street. The bell over the door rang the way it always had, and for a moment she stopped just inside it and couldn't go any farther.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks still lined the walls, their pendulums swinging together. On the workbench was the pocket watch he'd been repairing when the stroke took him. Its back was still open, and one tiny screw lay beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door stood in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat down at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands were shaking. She hadn't held tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers knew what to do. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown, and the watch started to tick.

At some point the sun had come through the fog outside. She hadn't noticed. She was listening to the watch, and under it all the others on the walls, the sound he had worked inside every day of his life. She missed him. The steadiness in her hands had been his before it was hers, and it had held for eleven years without her once asking it to.

Years later the shop still had his name over the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

The Harbor County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on Tuesday to approve a $48 million expansion of the Route 9 bus line. The plan adds 11 stops and extends service to midnight.

"This is about giving people a real alternative to driving," said Supervisor Lena Kowalczyk, who sponsored the measure. "For a lot of families in the east county, the bus is the only way to get to work."

Supervisor Mark Deaver cast the lone vote against. He argued that the plan leans too heavily on state matching funds. "If Sacramento pulls back, we're left holding the bill," he said.

A 2024 county survey found that 38% of east county households do not own a car. Ridership on Route 9 has grown 22% since 2022, to roughly 6,400 weekday boardings.

Construction is expected to begin in March, and the first new stops are expected to open by fall 2026.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and they aren’t well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

title: Rate limiting
sidebar_position: 4
---

Rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable, and the Gateway applies it per client.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. The header tells the client to back off for that long.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones work by destructive interference: they fight sound with sound. Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the ambient noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that is the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). The benefits appear to depend heavily on task type, and Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution that "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). Researchers need to examine the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes more closely.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. Her father was still in the shop, in the gears and springs and in the patience he had taught her. Grief, she understood now, was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still had his name above the door, and Nora wound every clock each morning, as he had.

A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable. This page explains how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and includes a `Retry-After` header indicating how many seconds to wait, so the client knows to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

These settings let you balance protecting your services against a smooth experience for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones might seem like magic, but they rely on destructive interference. They fight sound with sound instead of just blocking it.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the ambient noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that is the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, dramatically reducing what reaches your ears.

This technology works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

Understanding how this works can help you make a more informed choice of headphones.

final: The relationship between remote work and employee productivity remains a hotly debated topic in organizational research. Okafor et al. (2018) conducted a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A subsequent meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). These benefits appear to depend heavily on task type, though: as Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution, "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). These findings show the need for researchers to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

As the sun broke through the fog outside, Nora realized that her father had never really been gone. He lived on in every gear and spring and in the patience he had taught her. Grief, she understood now, was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.
