# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting keeps your APIs stable under load. This page covers how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header that says how many seconds to wait. Clients should treat it as a signal to back off, not just an error.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

Note that `burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Together, these settings let you balance protecting your services against keeping things smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but they run on a pretty elegant idea: destructive interference. They don't just block sound. They fight it with more sound.

Here's what happens. Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly pick up the noise around you. A dedicated chip then produces a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

It works best on low, steady sounds, like an airplane engine's hum or an air conditioner's drone, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, like a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also count on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

So noise cancellation is physics and engineering working together. If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like a bit of quiet, knowing how it works can help you choose better.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

When Nora finally went back to her father's shop, a thin fog was sitting over Delancey Street. The air smelled like rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had, and her chest went tight.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks covered the walls, all their pendulums swinging together, unhurried. On the workbench was the pocket watch he'd been fixing when the stroke took him. The back was still open, and one tiny screw sat next to it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door showed up in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said quietly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

Once he'd gone, Nora sat down at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers still knew what to do. She set the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch started to tick.

Outside, the sun was breaking through the fog, and it hit her that her father wasn't really gone. He was in every gear and spring, in the patience he'd taught her, in the steady beat of time itself. Grief, she understood now, was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, his name was still above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

If you spend much time on a computer, sooner or later you'll run into a task you wish you could automate. Maybe you need to search and replace across a pile of text files, or rename and reshuffle a bunch of photos in some complicated way. Maybe you'd like to build a small custom database, a specialized GUI app, or a simple game.

If you're a professional developer, you might be juggling several C/C++/Java libraries and finding that the usual write/compile/test/re-compile loop is just too slow. Maybe you're writing a test suite for one of those libraries and the testing code is tedious to write. Or maybe you've built a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a brand-new one for it.

He always makes me think of my poor Uncle Podger. You've never seen such a commotion in a house as when Uncle Podger decided to tackle a job. Say a picture had come back from the frame-maker's and was propped up in the dining room, waiting to be hung. Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, leave that to *me*. None of you need worry about it. *I'll* take care of all of it."

Then he'd take off his coat and get started. He'd send the girl out for sixpence worth of nails, then send one of the boys after her to tell her what size to buy. From there he'd work his way down the line until he had the whole house in motion.

"Now go and get me my hammer, Will," he'd shout. "And you bring me the rule, Tom. I'll need the step-ladder, and I'd better have a kitchen chair too. And Jim! Run over to Mr. Goggles and tell him, 'Pa sends his kind regards, hopes your leg is better, and could he borrow your spirit-level?' Not you, Maria, because I need somebody to hold the light. And when the girl gets back, she'll have to go out again for a bit of picture-cord. And Tom! Where's Tom? Tom, come here, I need you to hand me up the picture."

Then he'd pick up the picture and drop it, and it would slip right out of the frame. He'd try to save the glass and cut himself, and then he'd go leaping around the room looking for his handkerchief. He couldn't find it, of course, because it was in the pocket of the coat he'd taken off, and he had no idea where he'd put the coat. So the whole household had to stop hunting for his tools and start hunting for his coat, while he danced around them and got in the way.

# Rate Limiting

The Gateway limits how many requests each client can make in a given time window.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but they rely on a simple idea: destructive interference. They don't just block sound. They fight it with more sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like an airplane engine's hum or an air conditioner's drone, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden or high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly often, work remotely, or just value peace and quiet, knowing this can help you make a more informed choice.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). The benefits seem to depend heavily on task type, though. As Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution, "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). Researchers need to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner," Nora said.

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

As the sun broke through the fog, Nora realized that her father had never really been gone. He lived on in every gear and spring, in the patience he had taught her. Grief, she understood now, was just love with nowhere to go — until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

title: Rate limiting
sidebar_position: 4
---

The Gateway rate-limits requests to help keep your APIs stable and reliable.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait before retrying.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones work by destructive interference. Small microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, which sharply reduces what reaches your ears.

This works best on constant, low-frequency sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime, and her chest tightened.

Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. Her father was still there in the gears and springs, and in the patience he had taught her. Grief, she thought, was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door. Nora wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there's some task you'd like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you'd like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you're a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you're writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you've written a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and they are poorly suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use and available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, so it will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python lets you split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples when you start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules cover file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

Python is simpler to use and available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, so it will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python lets you split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples when you start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules cover file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting protects the stability and reliability of your APIs. This page covers how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and includes a `Retry-After` header indicating how many seconds to wait. Treat it as a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

These settings let you balance protecting your services against keeping things smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones feel a bit like magic, but the trick is plain physics: destructive interference. They fight sound with sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup keep sampling the noise around you. A chip then builds a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

It works best on steady, low-frequency sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz. The hum of an airplane engine and the drone of an air conditioner are good examples. A baby crying or a door slamming is much harder to cancel, since the sound is sudden and high-pitched. That's why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you're shopping for a pair, that's worth knowing. They'll tame an engine hum far better than a slammed door.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees, and those assigned to work from home performed 13% better. The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog sat over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Clocks covered the walls, dozens of them, pendulums swinging together. On the workbench was the pocket watch he'd been repairing when the stroke took him. Its back was still open. One tiny screw sat beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was proud of you."

Nora's throat went thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He used to say you had your own clocks to wind."

When he'd gone, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers knew what to do. She seated the screw, closed the case, wound the crown. It began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. Her father wasn't really gone, she thought, not with the patience he'd taught her still in her hands. Grief, she understood, was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later his name was still over the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

Years later his name was still over the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

If you do much work on computers, sooner or later you'll want to automate some task. Maybe you need a search-and-replace across a pile of text files, or you want to rename and rearrange photos in some tangled way. Maybe you'd like to write a small custom database, a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

Professional developers run into this too. You may be working with several C/C++/Java libraries and find the write/compile/test/re-compile cycle too slow. Or you're writing a test suite for one of them and the testing code is tedious. Or you've written a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a whole new one just for it.

Python is just the language for you.

A Unix shell script or Windows batch file could handle some of this. But shell scripts are best at moving files around and changing text data, and they're not well suited to GUI applications or games. A C/C++/Java program would work, but even a first draft can take a lot of development time. Python is simpler to use, runs on Windows, macOS, and Unix, and gets the job done faster.

You can split a Python program into modules and reuse them in other Python programs. It also comes with a large collection of standard modules, which you can build your programs on or use as examples while you learn. Some cover file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to GUI toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting keeps your APIs stable by stopping any one client from overwhelming them. This page explains how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and includes a `Retry-After` header indicating how many seconds to wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones can feel like magic, but they rely on a simple idea called destructive interference. They don't only block sound. They fight it with more sound.

Here's how it works. Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly pick up the noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

This works best on steady, low-frequency sounds, like an airplane engine or an air conditioner's drone, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also depend on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

So noise cancellation comes down to physics and engineering working together. If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like some quiet, knowing how it works can help you choose a better pair.

final: The relationship between remote work and employee productivity is still debated in organizational research. Okafor et al. (2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). These benefits seem to depend heavily on the type of task, though. As Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution, "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). Researchers need to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

As the sun broke through the fog outside, she thought of her father, still there in every gear and spring, in the patience he had taught her, in the steady ticking all around her. Grief, she understood now, was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you'll find there's some task you'd like to automate. For example, you may want to do a search-and-replace across a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you'd like to write a small custom database, a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you're a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle too slow. Perhaps you're writing a test suite for such a library and finding the testing code tedious to write. Or maybe you've written a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving files around and changing text data, and they're not well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time just to get a first draft working. Python is simpler to use, is available on Windows, macOS, and Unix, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python lets you split your program into modules that you can reuse in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples to learn from when you're starting out. Some of these modules cover things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. # Rate limiting

Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can send to your APIs, which keeps them stable and reliable.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Clients should treat it as a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Noise-cancelling headphones work by destructive interference: they cancel sound with more sound.

Small microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other and far less noise reaches your ears.

This works best on steady, low-frequency sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz, like an airplane engine's hum or the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden, high-pitched noises, like a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

Nora came back to her father's shop on a foggy morning. The fog lay thin over Delancey Street, and inside the place smelled of old brass. The bell above the door chimed the way it always had.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, pendulums swinging in unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he'd been repairing when the stroke took him, its back open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day. He was proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

When he'd gone, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years. Her hands were slow at first, then they weren't. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch started to tick, one more small sound among the forty or so on the walls.

Years later the shop still had his name over the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs, or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate limiting

The Gateway limits how many requests each client can send, which keeps your APIs stable and reliable.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header that tells the client how many seconds to wait before trying again.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Use these settings to balance protecting your services against a smooth experience for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones work by destructive interference: they cancel sound with more sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and much less reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot or work from home, knowing this can help you choose a pair.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). Researchers need to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in patient unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said softly. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat felt thick. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. Her father was still here, in every gear and spring and in the patience he had taught her. Grief, she understood now, was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.
reply:
This passage reads as human because it is. It looks like the opening of Uncle Podger's picture-hanging scene from Jerome K. Jerome's *Three Men in a Boat* (1889). I found no clusters of AI patterns in it: no negative parallelism, no trailing significance clauses, no banned vocabulary, no summary closer, no chatbot phrasing. The sentence rhythm varies, the details are specific (sixpen'orth of nails, Mr. Goggles, the handkerchief in the coat pocket), and the repetition is deliberate comic timing.

The only thing a pattern-matcher might flag is the em dashes in Uncle Podger's shouted dialogue ("Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom"). That is a character's speech and part of the joke, so I left it alone. Editing it would make the text less human, not more, so the final version is unchanged.
